column2: On the night of the fourth day of the New Year, the household welcomed the God of Wealth. Hu Xueyan’s extraordinary success during the past year had made him feel as though he had indeed encountered the god, and he burned the ritual paper offerings with unusual devotion. According to custom, women withdrew from ceremonies honouring the gods. As he stood alone offering incense and kowtowing, with neither brothers nor a son beside him, he was suddenly overcome by sadness. What lay beyond him seemed utterly empty. Even if the God of Wealth favoured him with a fortune of tens of millions of taels, what use would it be? When the god had been welcomed, the family gathered in the rear hall to share the blessed offerings. Old Mrs Hu was delighted, but her son looked melancholy. Forcing down two cups of wine and half a bowl of noodles in chicken broth, he put down his chopsticks and returned to his bedroom. “What is wrong?” his mother asked her daughter-in-law anxiously in a low voice. “On the very day we welcome the God of Wealth! He was still laughing and talking at dinner. Why the sudden change? Have you said something to him again?” “No. I haven’t said a word,” Mrs Hu replied. “At the beginning of a new year, we all want good fortune for the household. I wouldn’t pick a quarrel with him.” Her mother-in-law nodded repeatedly, much comforted. “I know how good you are. He owes his success to you too. But he has so much business outside, and entertaining is unavoidable. You must be more broad-minded.” All had been well until that last remark. It provoked a sharp resentment in Mrs Hu. She wanted to say that she was broad-minded enough already, but swallowed the words.

Back in the bedroom she found Hu sitting alone under the lamp, lost in thought. Remembering his mother’s words, she forgot the offending sentence and thought only of his many affairs outside. Her heart softened. He had built all this from nothing, with his own hands. At home she ought to give way to him. “You hardly ate,” she said. “There is rice porridge with red dates and lotus seeds. Would you like something sweet?” Hu shook his head, his eyes still fixed on the clear glass of the foreign lamp. “Then come to bed.” “Leave me alone,” he answered impatiently. “Go to bed yourself.” His cold response to her kindness hurt her. What was he thinking of? Naturally, that fox-spirit in Huzhou! Jealousy rushed straight to her head. Controlling herself with difficulty, she made the bed with tears in her eyes. Then Hu spoke. “Listen. I think you ought to consult a physician about childbearing.” She was astonished. “Why?” She dared not turn round, lest he see the traces of tears. “Why? There is nothing behind us but emptiness. Doesn’t that worry you?” He meant that she had borne him no son. Angry and distressed, she turned abruptly and stared at him.

“Bearing no son is one of the seven grounds for putting away a wife.” After staring a moment, she burst out with this. It was a heavy accusation, and Hu too was taken aback. “How can you say such a thing?” He was genuinely bewildered. He knew his wife had a mind of her own and was no ordinary woman, but had not expected words sharper than a knife. “Why shouldn’t I?” she asked with a faint, cold smile. “Having children concerns two people. Is there anyone in the world who can bear only daughters and never sons? Since that is what you say, naturally I must give way, and you can seek someone more capable.” It all came back to Furong. Recognising the cause, Hu could not help smiling. “You are capable enough yourself. First the blossom, then the fruit. I only meant that we might consult a physician who treats women and try a course of Fertility and Menstrual-Regulating Pills.” His wife was formidable indeed. She would not quarrel without reason, and now grew calm, but her words remained firm. Seizing the opportunity, she came to the crucial point. “And if they don’t work?” Hu was on his guard and dared not press his advantage. “Then they don’t work,” he said, sounding a little aggrieved. “If fate has decreed that I shall have no son, what is there to say?” Softness overcomes strength: those two apparently self-pitying remarks left her with no answer. That night they shared a bed but followed different thoughts. Mrs Hu considered the whole matter from beginning to end and made up her mind.

The next morning his mother asked, “When do you intend to leave for Shanghai?” “When the lanterns go up.” “Today is the fifth. There are eight days before then. There is still time.” “Mother!” Hu asked in surprise. “Time for what?” She explained that his wife wanted to visit her own family. They must count the days so that she could return before he left. Her family lived in Tangqi, a water town near Hangzhou. The journey there and back was tiring. If time was so short that she had to turn round almost as soon as she arrived, it would hardly be worth the trouble. “How strange! Why didn’t she discuss it with me first?” “I asked whether you knew. She said she must have my consent before telling you.” That explanation satisfied both courtesy and reason, but it was not how things usually happened. On every previous visit, husband and wife had agreed first and then informed their elders. Why was this time different? Besides, once the God of Wealth had been welcomed, merchants began giving their New Year dinners. Hu intended to entertain extensively over the next few days and needed someone to manage matters. How could she leave just now? When he explained this, his mother answered, “I mentioned that too. She said you would entertain at the shop and wouldn’t need her; she could be of no help there. As for the family dinner, the date has already been fixed. It is tomorrow.” “This is absurd!” Hu was annoyed. “Why wasn’t I told first?”

His mother already knew about Furong and felt her daughter-in-law had been wronged, so she was inclined to protect her. Taking the blame, she said the arrangement was her own idea and had nothing to do with Mrs Hu. Seeing how matters stood, Hu thought it best to say little. He gave a cold laugh. “Let her please herself. At home she is the one in command, anyway.” His mother naturally understood the implication. “This household depends on her,” she warned him. “Don’t imagine that because you are outside, nobody can control you and you can do whatever you please. If that is what you think, there is trouble in store for you.” Nobody knows a son like his mother. Her words went straight to his thoughts and made him wary. Yet on reflection he could not entirely suppress his grievance. “Mother, of the three failures in filial duty, leaving no heir is the greatest. Don’t you want a grandson?” “Of course I do,” she answered calmly. “Your wife and I have discussed it. She is a reasonable woman. As her mother-in-law, naturally I should follow her plan.” “What is her plan?” “Don’t ask yet.” His mother smiled. “It will be to your benefit.” Unable to guess what the two women were plotting, Hu could only leave the matter for the time being.

The next day they gave the family New Year dinner. Then Mrs Hu took her younger daughter, aged eight, and hired a boat for the journey to Tangqi. She was away only five days, returning to Hangzhou on the eleventh of the first month. The couple’s relationship had always been fairly good. After this short separation, their slight disagreement seemed forgotten, and they laughed and talked happily as before. Hu intended to leave on the fourteenth, so as soon as his wife returned she had to pack for him. He needed little personal luggage. The bulk consisted of local products to be given away in Songjiang and Shanghai. Besides Hangzhou’s “four specialities,” there were many kinds of food and useful articles. Sorting each gift separately was tiring work. These local goods had been obtained in bulk on account. Naturally, some were kept for the household. Hu opened a packet of crumbly sesame sweets made with lard and scented with osmanthus. After one piece he wanted no more. “Hezhu,” he called to his younger daughter, “come and finish these.” She picked one up, took a bite and shook her head. “I don’t want it.” “Why? Aren’t these your favourite sweets?” “They don’t taste nice. The ones from Huzhou are better.” “Where did you have sweets from Huzhou?” The question was really unnecessary: obviously, at her grandmother’s house. Yet it was like a drop of water falling into an oil bottle. Hezhu was old enough to understand a little of grown-up affairs. Suddenly she grew cautious, could not answer, and looked at her father with a flushed face, as though expecting punishment for some wrongdoing.

Hu’s suspicions rose at once. Seeing that his wife was not nearby, he took Hezhu to the window and asked quietly, “Tell Papa where those Huzhou sweets came from. When I return from Shanghai, I’ll bring you a foreign doll.” She did not know what to say. After thinking for a long while, she answered, “I don’t know.” This annoyed him, though he did not want to frighten her into tears. “Very well. If you won’t tell me, please yourself. When I return from Shanghai, your sister will have new clothes and a foreign doll. You will have nothing.” Between the threat and the reward, Hezhu finally told the truth. “Mother brought them back.” “Mother went to Huzhou?” “Mm.” She sounded aggrieved. “I wanted to go too, but she wouldn’t let me.” “Oh! How many days was she away?” “One day to go, one day to come back.” “Two days, then.” Hu thought a moment. “When she came back, what did she say to Grandmother?” “I don’t know. I went over to listen, and she sent me away. She also said I mustn’t tell anyone she had been to Huzhou.” Only now did Hezhu realise how serious this was. “Papa, Papa, you mustn’t tell Mother that I told you she went to Huzhou.” “I won’t, I won’t.” He gathered her into his arms. “I’ll buy you the foreign doll.”

Having reassured Hezhu, Hu was deeply troubled. Naturally his wife’s journey to Huzhou concerned Furong, but what she had done was hard to guess. Had she merely made inquiries, or taken some other action? He knew she had an excellent sense of measure and was nothing like a violent, unreasonable shrew. That made it all the more necessary for him to avoid rashness. He must plan before acting—or, as the saying went, meet soldiers with generals and floodwater with earth: discover her move and devise the proper answer. Once he knew her purpose and actions, he was confident he could deal with them. But this was a powerful opponent, and he must be careful. At home the odds were against him. His mother above and his two daughters below all stood on his wife’s side. One against four, he could hardly prevail. His immediate task was therefore to gain an advantage, and he could do it only in secret. If his wife learned of it, a little reassurance from her would make her position unshakable. First he sought Hezhu out again and warned her not to tell her mother what he had asked. Then he approached his elder daughter, fifteen-year-old Meiyu. She understood a good deal of the world. Though firmly her mother’s ally, she admired her father, so he adopted a different approach. “Meiyu, would you like to come to Shanghai with Papa?” The proposal surprised and delighted her. She longed to see something of the world, especially the foreign settlement with its countless novelties. Yet leaving her mother seemed unsettling. Her dark eyes moved to and fro, and for a while she could not answer.

“What do you think? Don’t you want to go?” “Who says I don’t?” Meiyu replied. “I’m a little afraid.” “Afraid? Then that settles it! I was hoping to rely on you, and you are afraid already.” “Rely on me?” She was utterly bewildered. “Papa, what could you rely on me for?” “To write things down and do calculations for me.” Hu sounded thoroughly serious. “My business outside has grown very large. I need someone to help, and it must be one of our own family. There are accounts nobody else can know about—not even Uncle Liu Qingsheng or Uncle Chen Shilong. I have thought it over, and you are the only person I can rely on.” This fabrication changed her feelings completely. Until now she had regarded herself as a frail girl, useless outside the home and fit only to help with household affairs. Suddenly she discovered that she could perform an important service. She felt grown-up at once. She stopped thinking of her mother, became bold, and saw no harm in venturing out into the world. But the first burst of courage faded under further reflection. “Papa, I’m afraid I won’t know how to keep the accounts.” “How do you keep the household accounts for your mother, then?” “Those are household accounts. Your money comes and goes in thousands and tens of thousands.” “Large or small, the method is the same. Household accounts are full of little items. Mine concern only a few things. They are easier to keep.” Encouraged, Meiyu’s ambition rose again. “Then I’ll go with you,” she declared. “But I must take A’cai.” A’cai was the maid who looked after her. Naturally Hu agreed, and the matter was settled.

Soon everyone in the household knew, though Mrs Hu supposed her husband was joking. “Are you taking Meiyu to Shanghai?” she asked. “Yes. She is growing up. I want her to gain some experience.” “Experience!” His wife was astonished. “They say the foreign settlement has bad ways. What experience is there to gain? If she comes home with bad habits, you will have ruined her.” Hu only smiled. What was amusing? A girl’s conduct affected her whole future. It was no laughing matter. He must be laughing at her ignorance! Mrs Hu resented it. “Am I wrong?” she asked, calmly but stubbornly. “Besides, they say the roads are unsafe. Meiyu is not to go.” “If the roads are unsafe, what about me? Aren’t you worried?” “You and Meiyu are different. With Master You looking after you, naturally I feel easy.” “Exactly. If she is with me, what is there to worry about?” Their words met point against point, needles hidden in silk, with all their force concealed. Yet Hu had gained the upper hand. Unable to defeat him in argument, his wife made one last move: she brought his mother into it.

With his mother he could not answer every objection so sharply. He returned to the story he had told Meiyu: he needed someone he could trust to keep accounts. This time the fabrication was more detailed. Some expenses for entertaining and social dealings had no receipts. Unless they were recorded at once, they became impossible to disentangle later. Nobody outside the family could be allowed to know these accounts, so he needed Meiyu’s help. Then he sighed. “If I had a boy, why should I have to take Meiyu? Even a nephew of my own would do. The trouble is that I have neither.” This was an inspired appeal to his mother’s feelings. She immediately began to think that, had Meiyu been a boy, at fifteen he could have gone out with his father to learn business. In five or six years he would be a capable assistant, and the growing enterprise would have someone to inherit it. Even if a boy were born now, more than ten years must pass before he grew up. That could not meet their present need. The Hu family had lost an opportunity. She could not help blaming her daughter-in-law for wasting all these good years. Once again Mrs Hu was at a disadvantage, and her husband was pleased with himself. But when he tried to discover more about her visit to Huzhou, he was disappointed. From what Meiyu said, her mother had told her nothing of it.

That evening a messenger came from the bank. Liu Bucai had returned from Huzhou and wanted Hu to come and speak with him. Obviously it concerned Furong. Otherwise, Liu was familiar enough with the household to call there himself. Having worked this out, Hu first watched his wife’s reaction. “How strange,” he said, sounding her out. “Why doesn’t Liu come here? Why must I go to him?” “Never mind that,” she answered with complete unconcern. “Go and find out.” Her composure was formidable indeed. Only when Hu met Liu did he learn that she had already seen Furong. She had simply introduced herself as the wife who had shared Hu’s hardships, left a five-thousand-tael banknote and taken her leave. “Such a thing!” Hu exclaimed. “I never imagined it.” “Nobody did.” Liu was embarrassed. “Furong sent me to ask your wishes before she decides whether to stay or go.” Hu returned to his former mode of address. “Third Uncle, please go back to Huzhou and tell Furong not to worry. I shall find a way.” “What way?” “I cannot explain just now. Whatever happens, I shall deal honourably with her.” This was precisely what Liu did not want to hear. Privately, he hoped Hu would give another twenty or thirty thousand taels, release Furong to find another home, and spare him this not altogether creditable connection through his niece. Hu’s words suggested the opposite. Disappointed, Liu could say little.

“How has your luck been over the New Year?” Hu asked, feigning leisure. This cheered Liu at once. “Excellent!” he said, grinning. “Victorious everywhere, with rich spoils.” He must have won a good deal. Hu thought this a suitable moment for advice. “Third Uncle, the pitcher is bound to break at the well, and the general is bound to die on the battlefield. Have you ever known anyone make his way in the world through gambling? You have a little money now. You ought to turn to serious work.” “All my debts are paid,” Liu replied. “I even won a deed to some land. I have asked Yu Si to arrange the transfer and put me in possession.” Then he grew reflective. “A man really cannot afford to be poor. Once he has a little money, people change towards him at once. In these last few days several people have offered to arrange a marriage for me, urging me to take another wife.” “That would be a good thing.” “There is no hurry.” Liu shook his head. “Let me enjoy a few carefree years first.” “That is wrong. Think of comfort before you have made your fortune, and hardship will come later. Third Uncle, I advise you to restore Shide Hall.” “What?” Liu was surprised. “Weren’t you going to have me help open Hu Qingyu Hall?” Hu had almost forgotten the undertaking himself. “Between ourselves, I shall tell you frankly. That must wait. Even if I open it, I shall have to find someone else. Third Uncle, your strengths lie elsewhere.”

This hurt Liu. “Xueyan,” he said reproachfully, “do you think gambling is all I can do?” “Not at all!” Hu felt apologetic and did his best to reassure him. “I know your abilities. There will be important matters in which I must depend on you.” “What about now?” “For now, it depends on your wishes. Your ambition was to restore the family business. That is why I advised it, and I can help you.” “My mind has changed. Even restoring Shide Hall would mean little. I certainly couldn’t stay behind a shop counter. I think I would rather go out into the world with you.” “Very well. First return to Huzhou and put Furong’s mind at rest. Tell her to live quietly at home and concern herself with nothing else. When I return from Shanghai, I shall make arrangements. Once you have delivered that message, come to Shanghai with Shilong.”

They parted with this agreed. Hu had already left the bank when an idea struck him. He had a five-thousand-tael note drawn and took it home. Finding his wife in the study, he handed it to her. “What is this?” she asked, pretending not to understand. “You gave away five thousand taels for nothing. I am replacing your private savings. Wouldn’t it be better to put your money in the bank and earn interest? Kept at the bottom of a chest, big money won’t breed little money.” His manner left her unable to fathom him. Their silent contest had reached its utmost limit. Uneasy, she thought that, since the secret was out, they had better speak openly. She began with an apology. “Xueyan, don’t blame me for not discussing it with you first. I had no choice. I did it for the whole family. We suffered for so many years, and now that your fortune has only just turned, you must not become entangled in love affairs. It was for your own good. After more than ten years of marriage, you know my heart.” She paused. “Of course, I have another plan, which I have discussed with Mother. You will understand in time. I am not an unreasonable woman consumed by jealousy.”

Those last words revealed her purpose to Hu. In any reasonably prosperous family, once a son passed thirty without a male heir, his parents began thinking of finding him a concubine. If another five or six years passed and the future remained uncertain, neighbours and clansmen would speak out in the name of fairness. Even the fiercest principal wife had to submit to the argument that leaving no heir was the greatest failure of filial duty, swallow her anger and let her husband take a second woman. Cleverly jealous wives therefore prepared in advance. They showed no anger and seemed positively eager to obtain a concubine, calling matchmakers in every few days. In collusion with them, on the pretext of selecting a woman whose appearance promised sons, they found a girl with broad feet and large hands, as stupid as an ox, to serve as the A’jiao of their husband’s golden house. As soon as she entered, they laid down countless rules. Commands within the women’s quarters were as strict as military orders; the concubine was treated like an enemy state, under such close guard that the husband could scarcely move. Hu considered his wife just such a formidable strategist and immediately declined the favour. “Don’t waste your plans. I shan’t thank you for them.” Then he turned to Furong. “Your journey to Huzhou was a mistake—a very great mistake. I told you it was a passing amusement, nothing to take seriously. I had my own way of extricating myself later. Now you have put me in a difficulty. If I follow your idea, give her a few thousand taels and send her away, everyone will say Hu Xueyan is afraid of his wife. Besides losing face, I shall make people think I cannot decide anything for myself. Tell me, will they still trust me?”

This argument left Mrs Hu stunned. Clever as she was, she had seen little of the world. How could she fully understand the habits and anxieties of business? She could only protest, “I went alone and came back alone. We met once, for less time than it takes to drink a cup of tea. Nobody could have known. Who would find out?” “Whether the spirits knew, I cannot say. But if you don’t want people to know of something, don’t do it. Never mind anyone else—I know already.” Hu deliberately stamped and sighed. “They are laughing at me in Huzhou now! Do you know what Pang said? ‘Running a great business is like an emperor ruling the realm. Execute whom you must, spare whom you should—everything depends on deciding at once. Above all, you must not let women hamper your steps. Yet it turns out Hu Xueyan must obey his wife! Suppose an opportunity arises and one immediate word decides between a fortune and the loss of all the capital. Then Hu says he must go home and consult his wife. Tell me, how can anyone join such a man in serious business?’” This invented speech made her turn pale and red by turns. Anxious and remorseful, she could not speak for a long time. Now Hu comforted her. “Don’t distress yourself. What is done is done. Regret will not help. For the moment, let them laugh. We will see when I return from Shanghai.” The more he spoke like this, the less reassured she felt. Disputes between husband and wife over a concubine invariably produced a storm. Even a good-tempered husband could not show absolutely no resentment. There must be some design behind it. And what had become of Furong? Had she withdrawn in the face of difficulty, or was she unwilling to let go? Mrs Hu needed a definite answer before deciding what to do. Now that the matter was out in the open, it ought to be settled cleanly. Waiting until his return from Shanghai invited further complications. Worse still, the resentment he might nurse throughout those days could change their relationship.

His business was important, Mrs Hu decided, but this was more urgent. She must ask him to remain. “Could you leave a few days later?” The moment she opened her mouth, as the saying went, he could see straight down her throat. He understood completely, but asked as though he did not, “Why?” “It is Meiyu’s first long journey. We must make her some more clothes,” she said by way of a pretext. “Two or three days’ delay would not matter, would it?” “If you say it won’t matter, it won’t.” He added an indirect warning. “But don’t cause me any trouble in those few days and make it impossible for me to leave. That would take half my life.” “What trouble?” Resenting her constant defeats, she complained, “No trouble can defeat you. Let each of us act according to conscience, that is all.” Her eyes reddened. Such weakness in a strong-minded woman is particularly moving. Hu felt a pang and put a hand on her shoulder. “After more than ten years together, don’t you know me? You have a conscience, and so do I. Otherwise we would not have reached the life we have today.” Thinking of that life made her more watchful and more certain she was right to keep him at home. She intended to ask Ji Heling to mediate and would concede whatever she could. Hu knew she meant to act, but not that this was her plan. Calm reflection showed him that their positions had reversed. At first he had carried a guilty secret and dreaded further questions. Now she was anxious and he was not. He could wait at ease, see what move she made and devise an answer in good time.

In this leisurely mood, with two or three extra days at his disposal, Hu suddenly felt like an outing. He invited Ji Heling and Qiu Fengyan to tour the lake by day, dine at Huangfan’er and then climb City God Hill to see the lanterns. Qiu accepted without hesitation. Ji declined the lake excursion but came to dinner. When the wine had warmed them, the conversation turned to Furong. One man was his sworn brother, the other a close friend with whom he could discuss anything. A little tipsy, Hu recalled his handling of his wife, felt pleased with himself and could not resist talking at length. That very morning Ji had been asked by Mrs Hu to mediate, so he was content to hear Hu make his own confession. Qiu knew nothing of this. Agreeing with Hu, he said, “Sister-in-Law Hu is indeed clever. She must have read the Code of Jealousy.” Hu had not understood. “What did you say?” “The Code of Jealousy—jealousy, as in envy; code, as in statutes.” “Wine has set you inventing stories again,” Ji said with a smile. “I have never heard of such a code.” “Naturally it is a literary jest, but not without reason. It depicts a principal wife’s jealous heart in the finest detail. Every man thinking of taking a concubine ought to read it.” Hu was interested. “Then tell us about this code.” “It has eight chapters: Personnel, Revenue, Rites, War, Punishments and Works, with Additional Regulations and the Statutes for Apprehending Offenders. There are citations and judgments. Admirable writing!”

“Recite a few provisions for us.” Qiu nodded, drank some wine and took a crisp “ringing-bell” roll, crunching it as he silently rehearsed the words. Then he suddenly laughed. “I remember! Here are two for you, from the military statutes: ‘Any wife who sees her husband enter a concubine’s room to converse and, on the pretext of household business, bursts in and breaks up their meeting shall be charged under the statute against unauthorised entry into a military headquarters. If she merely disturbs them without showing anger, the provision for mitigation shall apply: fifty strokes of the light bamboo, with no confession required. The judgment states: Before the jade-green bed, the parrot’s tongue is just being coaxed to speech; beyond the crystal curtain, suddenly comes the roaring of a lion. This is more than hanging washing over flowers: it suggests a sword concealed in the belly. If deliberate, the intentions are improper; if unintentional, the understanding is deficient.’” Hu understood these balanced phrases. “A fine judgment! Hanging washing over flowers—what a way to spoil the scene. She really deserves a beating on the palms.”

“There is another offence whose penalty is far from light.” Drawing out his voice, Qiu continued: “‘Any wife who judges that her husband and concubine are at a tender moment together, and suddenly calls the concubine away on another errand, shall be charged with unauthorised deployment of government troops...’” Before he finished, Hu burst out laughing. “Excellent! Unauthorised deployment of troops! What is the punishment?” “A hundred strokes of the heavy bamboo and military service on a distant frontier.” “Rather severe,” Ji said, laughing too. “You call it severe, but the author says, ‘To spare her life is already excessive leniency.’” Qiu went on with the judgment: “‘The battle is at its height, the rake enjoying a moment of spring; suddenly a golden tally recalls the troops, and the lady repeats her command three times. Once the siege of Baideng has been lifted, what hope remains of reaching Huanglong?’” “There is something in that,” Hu said. “What statute would a woman like my wife offend against?” Qiu considered. “There is this one: ‘Any wife who agrees to a concubine only because she has no choice, yet boasts of her virtue in hope of praise, shall be charged under the statute against an incumbent official erecting a monument to himself: one hundred strokes of the heavy bamboo and three years’ penal servitude.’ The circumstances are comparable, while the reputation contradicts the reality. ‘Usurping a reputation is prohibited; the regulations must be obeyed.’”

“Stop talking nonsense!” Ji felt that Qiu’s jokes were obstructing his work as mediator and prevented him from continuing. “My sister-in-law is nothing of the kind. Her wish to find Xueyan a concubine neither contradicts her real intentions nor usurps a reputation. Your Code of Jealousy does not apply.” Qiu caught the implication and adapted at once. “It is all fanciful nonsense, of course. Sister-in-Law Hu need not boast of her goodness. All her friends and relations know it.” “Every household has a difficult scripture to recite...” “Xueyan!” Ji interrupted. “What has become of your new favourite?” Hu had no reason to deceive him. “She is living quietly in Huzhou.” “Still under your name?” “Naturally.” Suddenly realising that Ji’s attitude did not entirely agree with his own, Hu asked, “Elder Brother, what do you think I should do?” “A thousand words come to one point: do not let this sow discord in your family. That would be a great misfortune.” “Exactly!” Qiu chimed in. “When the family is harmonious, everything prospers. Brother Xueyan, your good fortune is still rising. Now above all you need your wife’s help.”

Hu looked from one to the other and smiled. “Two fists cannot fight four hands. It seems I shall lose the argument today.” “Qiu is one of us, so I shall speak plainly. I have been asked to mediate. That alone shows your wife’s good sense. This morning I also paid my respects to your mother and received her personal instructions to settle this romantic lawsuit as your elder brother.” “Your mother’s command, your good wife’s request and your elder brother’s authority!” Qiu clapped his hands and laughed. “Brother Xueyan, you must surely obey.” Ji hastily waved him down. “That is not what I mean. Everyone is acting for Xueyan’s sake. First I want to know his wishes. His wife has told me that, provided they accord with reason and propriety, she will certainly meet them.” At this point Hu felt there was no need for further manoeuvres and spoke frankly. “I am not a dissolute man, nor have I reached a point where I can afford to be one. Having no son is one consideration; needing somewhere to rest as I travel is another. I therefore do not think that establishing a household in Huzhou wrongs my wife. I kept it from her out of respect. But she insisted on exposing the illusion, and now the play has become difficult to continue.” “It must continue even if you have to act with a stone mortar balanced on your head,” Ji replied. “Harmony matters most in a family. To achieve harmony, there must be forbearance. Your wife has shown it. What about you?”

“Haven’t I shown it too? I give way in everything and don’t quarrel with her. Surely I have treated her fairly.” “Yes, I know. But what about Furong? There must be some settled arrangement.” “The present situation is the arrangement.” “Then we cannot get any further.” Evidently Mrs Hu had imposed a condition. Was she still insisting that Furong be sent away? If so, there really was nothing to discuss. As they reached this deadlock, Qiu made a fair remark. “Both sides must yield something. It hardly seems right for Brother Xueyan to insist that everything remain as it is.” “Exactly! That is what I mean.” “And if it doesn’t remain as it is? Am I really to let everyone laugh at Hu Xueyan for being afraid of his wife?” “Certainly not,” Ji said. “I have understood your wife’s meaning. You may take a concubine, but she insists that you all live together.” “That is reasonable,” Qiu agreed. “Sister-in-Law Hu is within the bounds of propriety.” “It may satisfy reason and propriety,” Hu replied, “but there is still the law—the Code of Jealousy!”

This was an excuse without substance, yet not easy to answer with reasoning alone, unless Ji could offer a guarantee. Almost anything in the world could be guaranteed except peace between two rulers sharing a realm or two women sharing a husband. The difficulty vexed Ji, and he turned some of his annoyance on Qiu. “It is all your doing! Talking wildly about this Code of Jealousy and putting a weapon into his hands.” Good-tempered as ever, Qiu took no offence and accepted the blame. Pouring himself a cup, he drained it. “A penalty for me!” “Let me drink to you,” Hu said with a smile. “You did well to remind me.” “No, no!” Only now did Qiu realise that Ji’s complaint about giving Hu a weapon was no joke. He wanted no more of the subject. Waving his hands, he said, “Brother Xueyan, no more of the Code of Jealousy, or I shall become the chief culprit.” Hu merely smiled, looking entirely at ease. Ji felt something was amiss. As Hu’s sworn brother he could not evade responsibility; the family’s troubles were as much his concern as his own. He drank two cups in succession.

“Elder Brother!” Hu was quick to notice his displeasure. “Don’t trouble yourself. It is nothing so very serious.” “You don’t understand my position,” Ji sighed. “If you and your wife fall out, how could I ever face your mother again?” “We shall not,” Hu said firmly. “There will certainly be no rupture between us. Give a matter time and it can be settled. There is no need to hurry. Shall we leave it until I return from Shanghai?” Ji answered with a rueful smile. “What can I say? I only hope you mean what you say, bear your wife no resentment and listen to her advice.” “Where I can, I certainly shall. Where I cannot, I shan’t make her swallow an unbearable grievance.” There was nothing more to say, and they dropped the subject. After dinner they went to see the lanterns and returned late. Hu behaved as though nothing had happened, laughing and talking with his wife about the day’s excursions. The next day Ruiyun visited Mrs Hu with a message from Ji: Hu’s attitude had been excellent, the matter was sure to end satisfactorily, and she need not worry. These were words of reassurance. Unaware of the true state of affairs, and seeing no trace of resentment in her husband, Mrs Hu naturally believed the mediator’s message.
